title: Ch. 4 — Wisdom Sits in Places
paragraphs: The epigraph is Carson McCullers: to know who you are, you have to have a place to come from. Basso opens on a different note from the earlier chapters, with an argument about timing — that in an unsettled age of industrialism, forcibly uprooted peoples, legal efforts to secure sacred sites and new forms of environmental awareness, anthropologists still seldom study what people make of places. Then he goes back to the horses.

Four horsemen are camped at the end of a long day's work: Dudley Patterson, Sam Endfield, Charles Cromwell, and — arriving after three weeks away — Talbert Paxton, the youngest, an accomplished roper, normally restrained and plainly intelligent. He has spent those weeks drinking, pursuing love affairs, and spreading rumours about women who rejected him. Nobody mentions any of it. Dudley greets him instead with a place: so, you have returned from Trail Goes Down Between Two Hills. Sam adds: so, you have smelled enough burning piss. Talbert answers only, for a while I couldn't see.

Two Old Man Owl stories belong to that place. In one, the lustful and half-blind Old Man Owl is lured by two sisters and made to run back and forth between the two hills. In the other he tries to burn down the tree a girl has climbed, and she keeps putting out his fire from above. The diagnosis is unmistakable and never stated, and Talbert's reply — that for a while he could not see — is an admission that his moral vision had failed and has been restored. Basso lists the reasons the horsemen did not speak plainly: criticism would have insulted and condescended, since Talbert had reached those conclusions himself; none of them had the kinship standing to instruct him on his personal life, which belongs to his older matrilineal kinsmen; they were fond of him; and, beyond all this, they wanted the lesson attached to something concrete, fixed and permanent, that he had seen and could go to see again — a place upon the land. Their remarks were couched in the past tense, which let his resolve to change stand as already accomplished.

The chapter's real inquiry starts by accident. Dudley explains to Ruth Patterson that he has been telling Basso how the land can make people wise, and Ruth says firmly, in Apache: wisdom. It's difficult! The remark sends Basso into ethnographic gloom, and he admits he knows next to nothing about Apache conceptions of wisdom. In what does it consist? How would you detect its presence or absence? How is it acquired — taught, or arrived at alone? And why is it difficult? So he asks Dudley outright what wisdom is, and gets a faintly startled look and an answer: it's in these places. Wisdom sits in places.

What Dudley then delivers, quoting his grandmother, is the trail of wisdom — and he delivers it in a register close to Apache prayer, marked by grammatical parallelism, lexical redundancy, and the measured repetition of a few metaphors so densely compressed and probably so old that Basso says they stood well beyond his reach. Your life is like a trail, and you must be watchful as you go; you must see danger in your mind before it happens. You must make your mind smooth. You must make your mind steady. You must make your mind resilient. Each condition comes with exact consequences for its absence: without smoothness you fail to see danger and trust eyes that deceive you; without resilience you are easily startled and frightened, and stand in the way of your own mind; without steadiness you are angry, arrogant and envious, you gossip and criticize, and people come to despise you. You must learn to forget about yourself.

Basso then reconstructs the informal theory this rests on. Wisdom is a heightened mental capacity for detecting threatening circumstances when none are apparent; smoothness of mind is the primary condition, produced and preserved by resilience against distractions from outside and steadiness against distractions from within. The metaphors are precise: a smooth mind is cleared ground, an area free of obstruction; a resilient mind is a tightly woven basket, yielding but strong, an enclosed space that holds its shape. Because none of this is given at birth, wisdom exists in varying degrees, and only a few are ever completely wise. Two stories illustrate the failures — Coyote Pisses In The Water, where thirsty people would not wait for their leader and then panicked, and Grasshoppers Piled Up Across, where a proud medicine man insisted on singing alone while the corn was eaten. And the instruction to the young is a container metaphor all the way down, because the verb in the title applies only to rigid vessels and their contents: drink from places. Then you can work on your mind.
